blocks.heading: Betzilo chimadti: the sukkah as the shade of emunah

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach opens with the Zohar's reading of 'betzilo chimadti veyashavti' (Shir HaShirim 2:3) as the sukkah: a Jew longs all year to sit in the shade of emunah, under the wings of the Shechinah. He brings from Rebbe Shalom of Belz that the sukkah holds the holiness of the Beis HaMikdash, and so there is no contradiction with the Midrash that reads the passuk on the Beis HaMikdash.

blocks.heading: Yaakov Avinu, root of the sukkah

paragraphs.text: The holiness of the sukkah, the Mashgiach explains, comes from Yaakov Avinu, who made sukkos (Bereishis 33:17). As Rashi says at the beginning of Vayeitzei, the Beis HaMikdash came to Yaakov in chutz la'aretz, and so the sukkah brings it to every Jew. The Zohar recited before the tekios says that after appeasing Esav, Yaakov went to Sukkos, just as Jews enter the sukkah after Yom Kippur. The Zera Kodesh adds that the true sukkah is in heaven, and the sechach is its shadow.

blocks.heading: Sukkos, the Yom Tov of bitachon

paragraphs.text: Every Yom Tov, the Mashgiach says, has a segulah one carries through the year: yiras Shamayim from Rosh Hashanah, teshuvah from Yom Kippur, emunah from Pesach, Torah from Shavuos and bitachon from Sukkos. A person seeks security in a strong, weatherproofed house; Hashem tells him to leave it for a sukkah that rain and wind can enter, and to feel secure in Him. Citing the Ramban, he explains that bitachon is a level above emunah.

The Mashgiach brings the dispute in the Gemara (Sukkah 11b) on the passuk 'ki vasukkos hoshavti' (Vayikra 23:43): Rabbi Eliezer says clouds of glory, Rabbi Akiva says actual sukkos. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch follow Rabbi Eliezer, and the Bach explains that Targum Onkelos translates it as clouds of glory, and Onkelos received his Targum from Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, as the Gemara in Megillah says.

He then asks why the Rambam in his Peirush HaMishnayos limits the bad sign of rain to the first night. He answers with the Divrei Chaim: the sukkah must be one's address, so even when one steps out one still lives there, like a person who leaves a room when rain leaks through the roof. The first meal establishes the dwelling; if rain prevents it, the dwelling was never set up.

blocks.heading: The Rokeach: sukkos in the war with Sichon and Og

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach brings the Rokeach that Rabbi Akiva's actual sukkos were the huts the Jews lived in during the war with Sichon and Og, and asks what this has to do with the Exodus. He answers that both Tannaim agree the miracle was the protection of the clouds of glory, which no enemy could penetrate; Rabbi Akiva adds that it went with the soldiers out of the camp. Soldiers usually dig trenches against arrows, but the Jews built sukkos of straw that the sun shone through, knowing the clouds' protection was with them, a greater miracle.

blocks.heading: Teivah, Mishkan and sukkah: holiness by measurement

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach notes that the Torah gives measurements in three places: Noach's teivah, the Mishkan and the sukkah. Measurement, he explains, belongs to the lowest level, malchus, while above there is no cheshbon; a lofty light with no connection to this world can only be drawn down through a measured form.

The teivah separated Noach from a world under decree and placed him as if in heaven, where the decree did not apply. So too the sukkah's walls, measurements and sechach separate a Jew from this world; if a harsh decree remained after Yom Kippur, the sukkah lifts him above it. He adds that 'ki yitzpeneni besukko' (Tehillim 27:5) equals 'teivah' in gematria.

The Mashgiach recounts how Chizkiyahu went to sleep on Pesach night while Sanheriv's vast army besieged Yerushalayim, and that night the army was destroyed; Chazal apply 'ani shachavti va'ishana' (Tehillim 3:6) to him. His greatness was that he could sleep. So too one sits in the sukkah with calm security, able to sleep there.

blocks.heading: Lulav and esrog: bringing the light inward

paragraphs.text: Bringing the Arizal, the Mashgiach explains that the sukkah's light is too lofty to enter a person; waving the lulav and esrog in the sukkah and bringing them to the heart makes it inward. This is why Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai enacted taking the lulav all seven days as a remembrance of the Mikdash (Mishnah Sukkah 3:12), since the sukkah carries the Mikdash's holiness.

The Mashgiach brings pesukim showing that bitachon belongs to Yaakov: 'misgav lanu Elokei Yaakov' (Tehillim 46:8) and 'ashrei she'Kel Yaakov be'ezro' (Tehillim 146:5). Yaakov left his children the shade of the sukkah as an inheritance. According to Rabbi Akiva its protection moves from place to place, and so also from time to time, for the whole year and all generations. He describes Jews in Eretz Yisrael surrounded by hundreds of millions of enemies and saved by open miracles every day.

blocks.heading: The sukkah protects the world; bitachon brings simcha

paragraphs.text: A Jew's mitzvos, the Mashgiach explains, affect all creation: washing negel vasser removes the night's impurity from the whole world. So a Jew who exerts himself for the mitzvah of sukkah may protect thousands of Jews in Eretz Yisrael. Sukkos is the time of joy because simcha comes from bitachon (Tehillim 33:21); Hashem, he says, is our insurance policy.

blocks.heading: Simcha and somech; atzvus and azuv

paragraphs.text: The Mashgiach brings an approach that similar-sounding words in loshon hakodesh are related: simcha relates to somech, having a firm support to lean on, while atzvus comes from azuv, forsaken. He adds that Yaakov is the middle bar running through all levels, and that every Jew can climb gradually to some level of bitachon.

Bitachon, the Mashgiach says, must be lived. One should not rush davening for business but daven with a minyan that davens with chayus, even arriving later, since what is destined will come. One should not be curious in the street, and should not interrupt learning or a seudah for a telephone call; Hashem will provide greater earnings.

blocks.heading: The sukkah as Eretz Yisrael: judgment reopened

paragraphs.text: The Gemara (Rosh Hashanah 16b) places the sealing of judgment on Yom Kippur, while the Zohar extends it to Shemini Atzeres. The Mashgiach explains this with the Gemara in Makkos (7a): one who flees to Eretz Yisrael has his judgment reopened in its merit. Entering the sukkah is entering Eretz Yisrael and the Mikdash, so the judgment is heard anew.

In closing, the Mashgiach says that on Sukkos one draws emunah, bitachon and ruach hakodesh, which, following the Divrei Chaim, means being aimed at the truth of Torah. He urges taking simcha and bitachon for the whole year and davening with a minyan that davens with feeling. Bringing the Arizal, he explains that Sukkos draws chassadim that sweeten the judgments of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and he ends with a tefillah that Hashem rejoice with His people.
